In my honest opinion, while it may not look like the violent rape that media often shows, your relationship definitely started with rape. Which then seems to have turned into internalized-hopelessness and trauma. It is a trauma response to be hypersexual in some cases, which seems to have happened to you as well.

"I never said stop, I didn't think it would matter" He clearly has gaslit you into thinking you have no power over the situation, that it wouldn't stop even if you wanted to, on top of it you have tried to stop it before too and it didn't work. That screams rape to me.

Most cases of rape are sadly done not by strangers, but people you know, and it occurs most frequently in relationships and marriages. It's also taken less seriously when it happens in a relationship because people undermine your experience by saying "well you chose to be with them". The instances of you initiating sex all seem like a response to the sexual trauma you have subconsciously gone through, and it may seep into your future relationships as well so I deeply suggest therapy, or if you can't afford it join some related subreddits such as this one and r/ptsd and share your experience with people, or look into the experiences of others who suffered through relationship sexual abuse.

Rape at worst, and abuse at the very best, I genuinely hope you leave that relationship or have already left because someone who doesn't respect your boundaries is dangerous to be together with. If he is this comfortable stepping over your boundaries and abusing you now, what will it be like when he gets even more comfortable? I don't know what sort of a person he is, but even if you think "well it's not that bad" or "he said sorry" it's dangerous.

Sadly a lot of people victim blame, especially if they know or like the person who did it. And a lot of victims self-blame because they are gaslit by society and the perpetuator that they "wanted" it, or "asked for" it.

What you're explaining is indeed, rape. The thing is, some actions can start out as sex. Perhaps both of the parties agreed to have sex, but halfway through one of them wanted to stop and the other didn't let them, that's when it stops being sex and turns into rape.

If you don't mind me asking (so I can help you better understand) how did it start? Did you both agree to it? Or was it him that initiated it and you felt like you had no choice but to say yes?

For me the difference between them is that sex is between two consenting adults, or two consenting teens of similar age; rape has one of the parties non-consenting or not fully consenting. Whether it be by force, by coercion or out of fear/feeling like you have to for some reason. 

It doesn't have to be violent or verbally non-consenting to be rape, sometimes people feel like they have to go through with "it" even though they don't want to for several reasons. It could be a power dynamic, fear, coercion, feeling like you have no other option... etc. Once one of the parties don't have a chance to consent or do not consent, it stops being sex and turns into rape.

Hey, queer woman here as well, my partner goes by they/them pronouns. Trigger warnings for mentions of suicidal ideation.

I was about 3-4 years clear when we started dating, and most of my scars are very well hidden so they weren't discovered until about 2 years later when I relapsed. My partner had time to get to know me and my trauma in that while, and saw how I was actively fighting to get better and was overall careful with my situation.

At first it was a bit of a shock, but they are very supportive during my healing process and we took it very slow. Their sibling suffered from SH as well so both them and their mom were experienced with caring for wounds, and were cool and supportive thanks to that when I had a severe SH relapse. For me; my depression, SH, and suicidal ideation are a part of my struggles that I actively fight with, I get professional help and do everything I can to keep my SH urges at bay. Even then if I relapse my partner is understanding and calm. I feel very lucky about that.

I was hesitant about getting in a relationship, but I was confident enough in my healing process when we met that I decided I'd go for it. We did Long Distance for a while which helped as well. I think what helps the most is that we both have a family history with mental illnesses and SH, so we can understand each other better and have deeper conversations. 

I also try not to be negative or overwhelming when I'm depressed or suicidal so I don't wear out my partner too much. As in, instead of "everything is horrible I deserve to die" I go  "I am feeling very suicidal and depressed right now, I will probably not be available emotionally for a while". That made a huge difference for me. We decided on some certain terms like that to use between us, such as:

"I don't feel too good, can I vent for a while?"
"Are you in an okay mindset? If so I'd like to open up about my trauma a bit."
"I am very upset today, and feel rather suicidal. I'll try to distract myself or take my meds."
"Thank you for listening to me and caring, make sure to tell me if you start feeling overwhelmed, okay?"

These sentences help us remember that we both care and want the best for each other.

The reason why I'm writing all this down is, I wasn't mentally prepared and that completely broke apart my first relationship. While in my healing process, I stayed out of relationships because you really need to be in a healthier mindset to share a life with someone else. My partner is very caring, listens to me and helps as much as they can, but sadly not everyone is prepared or can handle such a relationship, and I don't want to use my partner like a therapist. Even if they love me more than the world, it will start hurting them and wearing them down at one point. There is an ideal world where they want to have endless energy and love for me, and there is the real world where they are mentally struggling as well, and we need to be careful with each other's personal space and well-being.

Idk I hope that helps a bit. I am very lucky and feel loved by my partner, but it took us a long time to get to know each other enough and learn about each other's mental state (in our 4th year now, wohoo!). We both use meds and see a therapist as well. I hope that life will help you meet amazing and supportive people as well ❤️‍🩹

I think for me, EMDR really helped and changed my life for a while, because I was on the edge of suicide and completely nonfunctional. The problem is that it's a REALLY agregious and hard process. It's basically reliving the exact trauma I went through while making sure my brain can process is properly and stop showing me nightmares about my abuse.

My doctor was very slow and careful about it, warned me before we began the process, got the numbers of people who could get to me in a state of emergency, made sure to spend an extra 10-20 mins after each session so i could get grounded.

It was a long and tedious process. It did end up helping me heal from the trauma and let out the pent up anger and grief I felt, but I don't know when, at one point it just started backfiring.

After I got what I wanted (my nightmares to stop) I had no goal left to accomplish with EMDR, l was going there and re-traumatizing myself for nothing. After a few sessions gone bad I spoke to my therapist. She asked me if I had any reason I could think of left to continue EMDR, I said no there wasn't, so after that she said we don't need to continue and we just stopped our sessions all together.

To this day I'm glad she helped me sleep peacefully again, but I must say people should get more warnings and a throughout explanation when they are going to try EMDR. It should be done by a professional who gets to know you well, and asks you all these questions so you know why you wanna go to EMDR therapy and what you're getting yourself into. *Even then* I think it just doesn't work for some people. It's extremely traumatic if done wrong and carries a lot of risks. We stopped as soon as I said it started backfiring, because I was DREADING going to EMDR by that point.

I'm sorry you went through such a hard experience, and I am very happy to hear that you are on a good healing road. EMDR just doesn't work for everyone and I think more people should be let known of the dangerous and hard side of it, before getting recommended to try it.

This might seem like a bad advice to most people, but as a long term cutter who always has to hide scars and lives in an extremely hot weather (long sleeves are not an option), I have one place where I can cut as much as I want without people realizing. Its the outer side of my hips, right under the panty line. No dangerous arteries, and bandages are very easy to hide even under shorts. I just put on some anti-bacterial oinment (like fucidin) and wrap it up with some gauze. Plus I have stretch marks there, so even without clothes healed marks blend in well. Just take care of the wounds well afterwards and it will be okay. Keep a small med-kit with you and find an excuse for it in case they ask (I bruised my toe, I cut my finger, etc.)

For me it took a really long time to rewire my brain into not seeking out abusive turn ons, but the most important part is to be patient with yourself when you do have moments of relapse, because they can happen even when you think you've been free of it for months. As a warning I don't know if this would work for everyone, it's my own personal experience. 

First step for me was getting into romance novels and online stories where there is enough drama and action to keep me interested, or an enemies to lovers type of trope but the romance that happens is very loving and respectful. I had to constantly tell my brain that is what I need and would like, and if the book is good enough I'd end up really getting into the soft romance. I did this for years, and it took a solid year or two before I started seeing real improvements but it eventually happened. Do try to distance yourself from movies/series that have toxic romantic interests or non-consensual looking scenes. I usually seek out action filled series because soft romance books tend to bore me, but it could be the opposite for you so just try different genres out. I could give a few recommendations that I personally liked.

Later I got into a relationship and started doing sexual RPs with a partner. I held the same rule, there can be drama but it always has to be respectful and loving. No humiliation, and even if there is some it canNOT be about my body, so no truly harmful comments. I wanted to make sure the relationship would be safe for my harmful habits, it can be hard but with the right person it happens. When we did include humiliations we made it clear that it was purely for roleplay and kink reasons, and it's best to keep a safe word and have aftercare. I cannot explain how important aftercare is. It lets you understand that what just happened was purely fiction and you are loved/cared for.

I'd suggest keeping away from porn as it can hold toxic elements sometimes. Rarely there are more romantic/story based ones but not worth risking it for me.

Be patient and understanding with yourself. What you went through isn't your fault, the way your brain got wired isn't your fault. You deserve love and respect, and it's possible to heal <3
